english.notes:
See H8685 for the Standard Offence Wording document relating to the substantive offence.
(i) A representation is false if it is untrue or misleading, and the person making it knows that it is, or might be, untrue or misleading (section 2(2) of the Fraud Act 2006).
(ii) Representation means any representation as to fact or law, including representation as to the state of mind of the person making the representation or any other person (section 2(3) of the Act).
(iii) A representation may be express or implied. That means it could be made in words or communicated by conduct. It could be written, spoken, posted on a website etc. or implied by conduct, for example by tendering a credit card a person represents that he has authority to use if for that transaction. This would also cover so-called 'phishing', where large numbers of emails are sent to people representing that they have been sent by a legitimate financial institution (section 2(4) of the Act).(iv) A representation may be regarded as made if it (or anything implied in it) is submitted in any form to any system or device designed to receive, convey or respond to communications (with or without human intervention). Meaning fraud can be committed where a person makes a representation to a machine and a response is produced without the involvement of a human being, for example by using a 'CHIP and PIN machine'. (Section 2(5) of the Act.)
(v) The test for dishonesty in all criminal cases is that established in the case of Ivey v Genting Casinos (UK) Ltd (trading as Crockfords) 2017, as confirmed in R v Barton and another (2020).
(vi) The offence requires an intention of making a gain or causing loss or risk of loss; the gain or loss does not actually have to take place.
(vii) Fraud can also be committed by failing to disclose information, section 3 of the Act and H8686, and by abuse of position, section 4 of the Act and H8687.(viii) Section 12 of the Act makes provision for directors, managers, secretaries or other similar officers or person purporting to act in such a capacity to be liable to prosecution where a body corporate has committed this offence.
(ix) When formulating charges different considerations must be made to those applied to crime recording (applying the Home Office Counting Rules).
